module_title: Business and Marketing of Fruit Juices

lessons.title: Market Research and Identifying Target Customers
lessons.body: Before you squeeze a single orange, you need to know who will buy your juice. Start by walking around your neighbourhood, local market, and bus park. Count how many people sell fresh juice. Note their prices, cup sizes, and flavours. If five people sell mango juice at 500 Naira per cup, you know the market is crowded. Look for gaps: maybe nobody sells ginger-pineapple blend, or nobody delivers to offices. Talk to at least 20 potential customers. Ask: What juice do you buy? How often? How much do you pay? What would make you switch? Write down their answers. For example, in Kano, you might find that students want cheap 200ml sachets at 100 Naira, while office workers want 500ml bottles at 500 Naira. That tells you to make two product lines. Also check who else sells similar drinks: supermarkets, kiosks, street hawkers. Your target customer is a group of people with similar needs. Pick one group to start: e.g., mothers in your church who want healthy drinks for their kids, or taxi drivers who need quick energy. Once you choose, focus your money and time on them. Don't try to serve everyone. Use a simple notebook to record your findings. After one week, you will have real data, not guesses. This research costs you nothing but time and will save you from making juice nobody wants.

lessons.title: Costing, Pricing, and Profit Margin Calculation
lessons.body: If you don't know your costs, you will lose money even when sales are high. Start by listing every single expense for one batch of juice. For example, to make 20 litres of orange juice: 30 kg oranges at 500 Naira per kg = 15,000 Naira. Sugar: 2 kg at 800 Naira = 1,600 Naira. Preservative (sodium benzoate): 100 Naira. Bottles: 40 bottles at 50 Naira = 2,000 Naira. Labels: 40 at 20 Naira = 800 Naira. Transport: 1,000 Naira. Gas or firewood: 500 Naira. Labour (your time): 2,000 Naira. Total cost = 23,000 Naira. That makes 40 bottles of 500ml. Cost per bottle = 23,000 / 40 = 575 Naira. Now add your profit margin. A common mistake is to add only 10%. For small food businesses, aim for 30-50% margin. If you want 40% margin, selling price = cost / (1 - 0.40) = 575 / 0.6 = 958 Naira. Round to 1,000 Naira per bottle. Your profit per bottle = 1,000 - 575 = 425 Naira. For 40 bottles, total profit = 17,000 Naira. But remember: you must sell all 40 bottles to get that profit. If you sell only 30, you still cover costs but profit drops. Always track your actual costs weekly. Prices of fruit change with season. In dry season, oranges may cost 800 Naira per kg, raising cost per bottle to 725 Naira. Then you either raise price or reduce bottle size. Use a simple exercise book to record every purchase and sale. At the end of each week, calculate your real profit. This habit separates successful juice businesses from those that close after three months.

lessons.title: Starting a Small-Scale Juice Business
lessons.body: You can start a juice business with as little as 20,000 Naira if you are smart. First, decide your production scale. Start with 10 litres per day. You need: a clean table, a sharp knife, a manual or electric juicer (manual costs 5,000-15,000 Naira), food-grade buckets, bottles, labels, and a cooler. You don't need a factory. Many successful juice sellers start in their kitchen. Next, get your legal basics: register your business name with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) for about 10,000 Naira. Get a food handler's certificate from your local government health office (often free or 2,000 Naira). Open a separate bank account for the business. Then set a daily routine: buy fruit early morning at the market (cheaper), wash and sanitise all equipment, juice, bottle, label, and deliver or sell by afternoon. For sales, start with people you know: family, neighbours, church members. Offer free samples to 10 people and ask for feedback. If they like it, ask them to buy a bottle and tell two friends. Use WhatsApp to take orders. For example, in Accra, a woman started by selling 20 bottles per day to her office colleagues. Within three months, she was selling 100 bottles daily and hired one helper. Reinvest your profit: 50% back into buying more fruit, 30% for equipment, 20% as your salary. Keep records of every sale and expense. Don't mix business money with personal money. After one month, review: What sold best? What time do customers buy? Adjust. The key is to start small, keep quality high, and grow slowly. Many fail because they buy expensive equipment before they have customers. You don't need a stainless steel tank on day one. You need customers.

lessons.title: Branding, Packaging Design, and Labeling for Retail
lessons.body: Your brand is what makes customers choose you over the next seller. Start with a simple name that is easy to remember and say. Avoid long names. 'Mama Ada Juice' is better than 'Ada's Freshly Squeezed Natural Fruit Juice Enterprise'. Create a logo: you can pay a local artist 5,000 Naira to draw a fruit with your name. Use bright colours: orange for orange juice, green for pineapple, red for watermelon. Your packaging must protect the juice and look clean. For small scale, use clear PET bottles with screw caps. A 500ml bottle costs 50-80 Naira. For a more premium look, use glass bottles (200 Naira each) but you must collect them back. Labels are critical. By law in most African countries, your label must show: product name, ingredients (in descending order by weight), net volume (e.g., 500ml), your business name and address, batch number, production and expiry dates, and storage instructions (e.g., 'Keep refrigerated after opening'). Also include a phone number. Print labels at a local print shop: 1,000 labels cost about 15,000 Naira (15 Naira each). Design your label with a bold fruit image and your logo. Use a font that is easy to read from one metre away. Don't lie: if you add water, say 'juice drink' not '100% juice'. If you add preservative, list it. Customers trust honesty. For retail, you need a barcode if you want to sell in supermarkets. GS1 barcodes cost about 50,000 Naira per year, so start with direct sales to shops that don't require barcodes. Finally, make your bottles consistent: same size, same label position, same fill level. Inconsistent packaging looks amateur. A neat, well-labelled bottle can sell for 200 Naira more than an unlabelled one.

lessons.title: Marketing Strategies: Social Media and Farmers Markets
lessons.body: You don't need a big budget to market your juice. Start with WhatsApp. Create a WhatsApp Business account (free). Upload your logo, set your hours, and add a catalogue with photos and prices. Send a broadcast message to all your contacts once a week with a special offer, e.g., 'Buy 5 bottles, get 1 free this Friday.' Ask happy customers to send a voice note or text testimonial. Post those on your status. For Facebook and Instagram, post three times a week: a photo of you squeezing fruit, a short video of a customer drinking, and a price list. Use hashtags like #FreshJuiceLagos #HealthyDrinksAccra. Respond to every comment and message within one hour. For farmers markets, book a stall. In Nairobi's City Market, a stall costs 1,000 Ksh per day. Bring free samples in small cups. Let people taste. Have a sign with your price and phone number. Offer a 'market special': 2 bottles for 1,500 Naira instead of 1,800. Collect phone numbers of buyers and add them to your WhatsApp list. Partner with other vendors: a baker can sell your juice with their cakes. Give them 10% commission. Also approach small shops, salons, and gyms. Offer to supply them on consignment: they pay you after they sell. Leave 10 bottles. Check back in two days. If they sold, restock. If not, take back and try another shop. Use a simple customer list: name, phone, what they buy, how often. Send a 'We miss you' message to anyone who hasn't bought in two weeks. Word of mouth is your best marketing. One satisfied customer tells five people. One angry customer tells twenty. So always deliver on time and never sell spoiled juice.

lessons.title: Regulatory Compliance and Licensing for Juice Sales
lessons.body: Selling juice without following health rules can get you shut down, fined, or worse, make people sick. In most African countries, you need at least three things: business registration, health certificate, and food safety compliance. Start with business registration. In Nigeria, register with CAC as a sole proprietorship for about 10,000 Naira. In Kenya, register with eCitizen for 1,000 Ksh. In Ghana, register with the Registrar General's Department for 50 GHS. This gives you a legal name and tax ID. Next, get a food handler's certificate. Your local government health office or ministry of health issues this after you and your workers take a short course on hygiene. It costs 2,000-5,000 Naira and must be renewed yearly. They will inspect your kitchen: you need clean water, a handwashing station, a fridge, and separate areas for raw fruit and finished juice. You also need a laboratory test for your juice. Take a sample to a government lab or private lab (e.g., in Lagos, the Lagos State Environmental Protection Agency lab). They test for bacteria like E. coli and salmonella. A test costs 10,000-20,000 Naira. If your juice passes, you get a certificate. Then you need a product registration number from NAFDAC (Nigeria) or equivalent (FDA in Ghana, KEBS in Kenya). This can take 3-6 months and cost 50,000-100,000 Naira. Many small sellers start by selling locally without NAFDAC, but you cannot sell in supermarkets without it. Always label your juice with production and expiry dates. Keep records of every batch: date made, fruit source, preservative used. If a customer complains, you can trace the problem. Finally, pay your taxes. Even small businesses must pay a presumptive tax. In Nigeria, turnover under 25 million Naira pays 0.5% tax. Compliance may seem expensive, but it builds trust and opens bigger markets.

quiz.q: What is the first step in market research for a juice business?
options: B) Walk around and count existing juice sellers
quiz.explanation: Walking around and counting competitors gives you real data on prices and gaps before you invest.

quiz.q: How many potential customers should you talk to when starting market research?
quiz.explanation: Talking to at least 20 people gives you a reliable picture of what customers want.

quiz.q: In the costing example, what is the cost per 500ml bottle of orange juice?
quiz.explanation: Total cost of 23,000 Naira divided by 40 bottles equals 575 Naira per bottle.

quiz.q: What profit margin should a small juice business aim for?
quiz.explanation: A 30-50% margin covers unexpected costs and allows reinvestment.

quiz.q: If cost per bottle is 575 Naira and you want a 40% margin, what is the selling price?
quiz.explanation: Selling price = cost / (1 - margin) = 575 / 0.6 = 958 Naira.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a simple exercise book for your juice business?
options: B) To record every purchase and sale
quiz.explanation: Recording all transactions helps you calculate real profit and adjust prices.

quiz.q: What is a recommended starting production scale for a small juice business?
quiz.explanation: Starting with 10 litres per day is manageable and allows you to test the market.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT needed to start a small juice business?
quiz.explanation: A stainless steel tank is expensive and not necessary for starting small.

quiz.q: How much does it cost to register a business name with CAC in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: CAC registration for a sole proprietorship costs about 10,000 Naira.

quiz.q: What percentage of profit should be reinvested into buying more fruit?
quiz.explanation: Reinvesting 50% of profit ensures you can buy enough fruit to grow.

quiz.q: Why is it important to separate business money from personal money?
options: B) To know your true profit and loss
quiz.explanation: Mixing money makes it impossible to know if your business is actually profitable.

quiz.q: What is a good brand name for a juice business?
options: A) Ada's Freshly Squeezed Natural Fruit Juice Enterprise
C) The Best Juice in the World Company
quiz.explanation: Short, memorable names like 'Mama Ada Juice' are easier for customers to recall.

quiz.q: What must be included on a juice label by law?
options: B) Ingredients in descending order by weight
quiz.explanation: Ingredients must be listed from most to least by weight for consumer safety.

quiz.q: What is the cost of 1,000 printed labels at 15 Naira each?
quiz.explanation: 1,000 labels multiplied by 15 Naira equals 15,000 Naira.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid lying on your label?
options: A) It is illegal and customers will not trust you
B) It makes the label too long
C) It costs more to print
quiz.explanation: Honest labelling builds trust and is required by law.

quiz.q: What is a barcode used for in retail?
options: A) To make the bottle look nice
B) To allow supermarkets to scan and track products
quiz.explanation: Barcodes are required by supermarkets for inventory and checkout systems.

quiz.q: What is a good social media platform for a small juice business to start with?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp Business is free, widely used, and allows direct communication with customers.

quiz.q: How often should you post on Facebook or Instagram for your juice business?
quiz.explanation: Posting three times a week keeps customers engaged without overwhelming them.

quiz.q: What is a 'market special'?
options: B) A discounted price for buying at the market
quiz.explanation: A market special is a limited-time discount to attract customers at a farmers market.

quiz.q: How much commission should you offer a baker who sells your juice?
quiz.explanation: A 10% commission is a fair incentive for partners to promote your juice.

quiz.q: What is consignment selling?
options: B) Giving bottles to a shop and getting paid after they sell
quiz.explanation: Consignment means the shop pays you only after the product is sold, reducing their risk.

quiz.q: Why is word of mouth important for a juice business?
options: B) It is the only way to sell
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Satisfied customers tell others, bringing new customers at no cost.

quiz.q: Which document is NOT required to legally sell juice?
quiz.explanation: A driver's licence is not relevant to food safety or business registration.

quiz.q: How much does a food handler's certificate typically cost?
quiz.explanation: The certificate is affordable, usually between 2,000 and 5,000 Naira.

quiz.q: What does a laboratory test for juice check for?
options: B) Bacteria like E. coli and salmonella
quiz.explanation: Lab tests ensure your juice is free from harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: Which agency regulates food and drugs in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC is responsible for registering and regulating food and drug products in Nigeria.

quiz.q: How long can it take to get NAFDAC product registration?
quiz.explanation: NAFDAC registration typically takes 3 to 6 months.

quiz.q: What is a presumptive tax?
options: A) A tax on profits only
B) A tax based on turnover for small businesses
quiz.explanation: Presumptive tax is a simplified tax for small businesses based on turnover.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of every batch of juice?
options: B) To trace problems if a customer complains
quiz.explanation: Batch records help you identify and fix issues if a customer gets sick.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do before selling juice to the public?
options: B) Get a health certificate and lab test
quiz.explanation: Health certificate and lab test ensure your juice is safe and legal to sell.
